chapter: Reading, repertoire and New Orleans players
title: Credit due to the New Orleans Rhythm Kings and Rappolo
summary: He argues the Rhythm Kings deserve more credit and describes Rappolo's clarinet style.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: They were good numbers, just like when a guy wants a kid around and play slapsticky. And we played the St. Louis Blues, and they played... That kind of chorus that Larry Shields played. It was a corny figure, you know what I mean? Yeah. I always put that in. But the band that I think that your company there will achieve, the business, Tulane, and this place that's out on the end of Espinade, what is that? The Old Mint.
What they should do is give more credit to the original New Orleans rhythm kings.

Now, they gotta... Everybody tries to play like... Like... Like... Like... Like... Rip Haller. You understand? He played more clarinet than Benny Goodwin, all his catch. You understand? All the other guys... I mean, Benny Goodwin's a technician. Mm-hmm. You understand? Benny Goodwin played... He tried to play that way, but he can't... It's a different feel for him. So, he played... He can read music and everything else and all. Mm-hmm. He played in all his show and all. He played his way, see? But Rap had... Had a style that... That... You know, I don't know how to... How to explain it. People... Like Sidney Aaritan, you know, and stuff like that. Mm-hmm. That's the way Rap played. And then Paul played the right kind of leads for these guys. Mm-hmm. And George Aburnus on trombone. I got a picture of George Aburnus. Yeah. Who played this jazz concert over here in Curveville. And they had... Had Max... Max... Max Kaminsky playing... We'll call it. And... Different things. Anyway... Those guys... They... They... The tunes that the bands in New Orleans played... Now, I like to play... That's a plenty. Now, you know... Lou Pollock... Is a piano player. Mm-hmm.
